title: Celestial Bodies
author: Dimitris Yfantidis
summary: A thousand textured spheres pulling on each other with gravity, drawn with instanced OpenGL.
description: A thousand textured spheres scattered through a spherical shell around the origin, each pulling on every other with Newton's law of gravity. They start at rest: hold = to speed up time and watch them fall together. They are drawn in instanced batches with OpenGL 3.3 and lit by a point light at the centre.
how_it_works: Every frame, each body's acceleration is the sum of the gravitational pulls of all the others (G m / r squared), about a million pairs for 1,000 bodies, computed on one CPU core. Velocities and positions then advance by the frame's time step, multiplied by the simulation speed.

One sphere mesh (32 x 64 segments, about 4,000 triangles) is uploaded to the GPU once. All 1,000 spheres are drawn from it with instanced rendering: each glDrawElementsInstanced call draws up to 500 copies, and the vertex shader moves and scales every copy using its instance number to look up a position and a radius.
Lighting is diffuse (Lambert) shading from a point light at the origin plus a little ambient light, applied to a texture of a fictional Ceres-like surface.
The bodies sit at random directions and distances (20 to 400 units) from the origin; the camera orbits that point in spherical coordinates.
highlights: A thousand spheres from just two draw calls per frame.
Hold = to speed up time: the bodies start at rest and slowly fall towards each other.
The sides facing the centre are lit; the far sides fall back to the ambient light.
Zoom out with numpad minus to see the whole shell of bodies.
controls: Speed up / slow down the simulation
